body.heading: A camper's rule for everywhere
paragraphs: Campers are taught to leave a site cleaner than they found it. The rule travels well beyond campsites: to parks, beaches, shared kitchens, hire cars, borrowed flats, and the bench outside the café. It asks for minutes and returns places to strangers in better shape than you received them.
The smallest version is portable: pick up one piece of litter that is not yours, wipe the table you used, push the chairs back in. Multiply by everyone and the maths is lovely.

body.heading: Invisible kindness, visible places
paragraphs: Leaving things better is usually anonymous — nobody sees you straighten the books on the train or return the stray trolley — and that is part of its character. It is kindness as maintenance rather than gift: unglamorous, unthanked, and load-bearing.
Children learn it fast when it is framed as a game: how many things can we leave better today? A gate closed, a tap turned off, a lost glove placed on a fence post where its owner will pass.

body.heading: It includes people
paragraphs: The rule applies to situations as well as places. Leave the meeting calmer than you found it, the group chat friendlier, the queue more patient. Rooms and relationships both respond to being left better.
Start with the easiest square metre: the bit of pavement, desk, or kitchen you will touch today. Better is a direction, not a standard, and directions are walkable.

description: The camper's rule — leave a place cleaner than you found it — turns out to work for shared kitchens, group chats, and meetings too.
